sections.title: Definition: fever, PUO and the look-alikes

blocks.text: **Fever** means a **core temperature above 38.0°C**. It is driven by cytokines and acute phase proteins, so it appears in **non-infective as well as infective** disease. Feeling hot or sweaty does not count: fever is diagnosed only from a **recorded** reading. Oral and rectal readings are more accurate than axillary or ear readings.

blocks.title: How the books define pyrexia (fever) of unknown origin
rows: 1 week of in-hospital investigation without a diagnosis
3 days as an inpatient, **or** 3 outpatient visits, **or** 1 week of intensive ambulatory work-up
Intelligent, intensive investigation; known HIV or other immunosuppression is usually excluded
1 week in hospital or 3 outpatient visits

blocks.text: Davidson recognises **subsets** of PUO: **HIV-1-related**, **immune-deficient** and **nosocomial** PUO. These, like travel-related fever, have their own work-up beyond the standard first-line tests.

blocks.title: Things that mimic or hide fever
items: **Sweating with a normal temperature**: alcohol, anxiety, thyrotoxicosis, diabetes, acromegaly, lymphoma and a hot environment.
**Night sweats** with true fever suggest **TB** or **infective endocarditis**.
**Exaggerated circadian variation**: some healthy people run an evening peak that is harmless. Confirm a genuine fever first, by admission for observation if needed.

**Hyperthermia** (heat stroke, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia): the hypothalamic set-point is **unchanged** and the body cannot shed heat, so antipyretics do **not** work. In true fever the set-point is raised.
**Blunted fever**: end-stage renal or liver disease, the very young or old, protein-calorie malnutrition, immunosuppression and steroids. Chart a fever curve while antipyretics are held.

blocks.text: PUO is a **label of exclusion**, not a diagnosis. It is usually an **unusual presentation of a common disease** rather than a rare disease, so keep investigating until a cause appears.

The books disagree on the definition. **Davidson** uses **>38.0°C for >3 weeks**, Kumar & Clark use **>2 weeks**, and the US books use a **38.3°C** cut-off. For this course, follow Davidson: a fever of 38.1°C still qualifies, but 10 days of fever does not.

sections.title: Causes of PUO: the five groups

blocks.title: Davidson's aetiology of PUO (★ = commonest in the group)
rows: Abscesses (hepatobiliary, diverticular, urinary including prostate, lung, CNS); dental and sinus infection; bone and joint infection; **infective endocarditis★**; **TB, especially extrapulmonary★**; HIV, CMV, EBV; fungi; fastidious organisms (Bartonella, _Tropheryma whipplei_)
**Lymphoma★**, leukaemia, myeloma; solid tumours of kidney, liver, colon, stomach and pancreas
Older adults: **temporal arteritis/PMR★**. Younger adults: **Still's disease★**, SLE, vasculitis (PAN, GPA), polymyositis, Behçet's, rheumatic fever where endemic

Atrial myxoma, aortitis; sarcoidosis, PE; IBD, granulomatous hepatitis; thyrotoxicosis, phaeochromocytoma, adrenal insufficiency; PNH, TTP, Castleman's; familial Mediterranean fever; **drug reactions★**; factitious fever
No cause found despite full work-up

blocks.title: Clinical clues that point to a cause
items: **Giant cell arteritis/PMR**: headache, tender scalp, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, aching muscles and a high ESR.
**Adult-onset Still's disease**: a fleeting truncal rash, lymph node enlargement, sore throat and a **very high ferritin**.
**Lymphoma**: lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, low haematocrit or platelets and a raised LDH.
**Renal cell carcinoma**: microscopic haematuria with a **raised** haematocrit.
**Atrial myxoma**: obstructive symptoms, emboli and constitutional upset.
**Familial Mediterranean fever**: bouts of fever with peritonitis and pleuritis, raised WBC and ESR during attacks, and often a family history.
**Drug fever**: antibiotics, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, barbiturates, quinidine, procainamide, hydralazine and methyldopa. Always ask **when each drug was started** relative to the fever.

blocks.text: **Disseminated or extrapulmonary TB** can have a normal chest X-ray, a negative IGRA or tuberculin test and negative sputum smears. Tissue biopsy (lung, liver or marrow) looking for granulomas yields **80–90%** in miliary disease.

If blood cultures stay negative in suspected endocarditis, think of **Coxiella** and **Bartonella**, the leading culture-negative organisms along with streptococci. HACEK organisms now usually grow within 3–5 days with modern culture systems.

Step-Up claims that **idiopathic** PUO is now the commonest category. Davidson puts **infection (~30%)** as the largest group, with ~15% idiopathic, and Kumar & Clark agree that occult infection remains commonest in adults. For SBA questions, **infection is the commonest identifiable cause**. Davidson's own undiagnosed figure varies: "up to one-third" in one place, ~15% in the box and ~10% in the prognosis section.

sections.title: Special groups and the factitious patient

blocks.title: Who is likely to have what
rows: Infection, especially **viral**. Periodic fever syndromes if there is a family history

**TB**, intra-abdominal abscess, complicated UTI, endocarditis, **PMR/temporal arteritis** and tumours. Fewer cases stay undiagnosed than in the young; rheumatic disease makes up about a third in older adults (First Aid)

Malaria, dengue, rickettsiae, brucellosis, amoebic liver abscess, enteric fever, leishmaniasis, **melioidosis** (_Burkholderia pseudomallei_, South-east Asia), **MERS-CoV** (Arabian Peninsula), _Trypanosoma cruzi_ (Central and South America)
Pneumonia, infected prosthetic material or surgical sites, UTI, central venous catheter infection

Acute retroviral syndrome; AIDS-defining infections such as **disseminated MAC**, _Pneumocystis_ pneumonia and **CMV**; also histoplasmosis. Over 75% of causes are infectious, but HIV itself is rarely the culprit
Soft tissue and respiratory infections are commonest; look for endocarditis, injection-site abscesses and ilio-psoas abscess

blocks.title: Fever in old age: traps
items: Oral temperatures are **unreliable**, so fever can be missed. Rectal or eardrum readings are better.
**Delirium** often accompanies fever, especially with dementia or cerebrovascular disease.
Stroke and thromboembolism can cause fever, but **co-existing infection must still be excluded**.

blocks.title: Clues to factitious fever (Davidson Box 11.3)
items: The patient **looks well**.
An odd chart: **no diurnal variation**, and the **pulse does not rise** with the temperature.
Readings **above 41°C**.
**No sweating** as the temperature falls.
**Normal ESR and CRP** despite "high fever".
Signs of self-injection or self-harm, and a **normal reading when measurement is supervised**.
Infection with **several commensal organisms** (gut or mouth flora), e.g. from injected material.

blocks.note: Look at: fever in the injection drug user. Splinter haemorrhages and Roth's spots (endocarditis), injection-site abscesses, and hip flexor spasm with a positive femoral stretch test in ilio-psoas abscess.

blocks.text: In men, remember the **prostate** as a hidden source. In older men, send urine for culture **after prostatic massage**.

Factitious fever (switching thermometers, injecting pus or other contaminated material) is a **diagnosis of exclusion**. A mixed growth of bowel or mouth organisms in blood should raise the suspicion, not end the work-up.

**Repeat the history and the examination regularly.** Ask about every drug and when it was started, travel, occupation, hobbies, animals, sexual exposures, TB contacts, immunisations and family history. Examine teeth, eyes, heart (murmurs), abdomen (hepatosplenomegaly, tenderness), skin, lymph nodes, joints, breasts, spine and testes. New signs, such as a rash or stigmata of endocarditis, can appear later.

blocks.title: First-line tests (Davidson)
items: FBC with differential, **including the eosinophil count**.
U&E, LFTs, glucose and muscle enzymes (CK).
ESR and CRP.
HIV antibody test and autoantibodies including **ANA**.
Chest X-ray and ECG.
Urinalysis and urine culture; **blood cultures**; throat swab for culture or PCR.
In endemic regions: **malaria films on 3 consecutive days** (or a rapid antigen test), **dengue NS1 antigen**, blood cultures for _Salmonella_ Typhi and abdominal ultrasound.

blocks.text: Take **at least three sets of blood cultures** from different sites, **before antibiotics**, and repeat them. Ask the lab for **prolonged incubation** when exposure suggests a slow grower such as _Brucella_. Serial CRP measurements track progress.

blocks.title: If the first round is negative
items: Induced sputum or other samples for **mycobacterial stains and culture**.
Serology (including HIV) and **ferritin**.
Abdominal **ultrasound or CT**. US texts advise CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis early in true FUO to find tumours and abscesses.
**Echocardiography** for endocarditis.
Box 11.5 extras: autoantibodies, complement, immunoglobulins, cryoglobulins; CT/MRI; plain films, spinal imaging and bone scan; **labelled white-cell scan**; **PET/SPECT**.
Serology for less common organisms (_Brucella_, _Coxiella_, _Bartonella_) case by case.

blocks.title: Targeted tissue sampling
columns: When to use it and what it finds
rows: Biopsy of a lesion seen on imaging
Culture, histology and nucleic acid tests. **16S rRNA analysis** helps when earlier antibiotics stop organisms growing
Yield **up to 15%**: haematological malignancy, myelodysplasia, TB; also brucellosis, typhoid, visceral leishmaniasis. **Send marrow for culture** as well as microscopy
Only if bloods or imaging are abnormal (e.g. high ALP); finds granulomatous hepatitis
Consider in anyone **over 50**, even with **no physical signs and a normal ESR**
Excision preferred; lymphoma may need **more than one** biopsy
Test of choice for **visceral leishmaniasis** (specialist centres)

blocks.title: Reading the clues in the results
items: Raised liver enzymes point to the **liver or biliary tree**.
Raised CK suggests **myositis** or a drug effect.
A **markedly raised ferritin** suggests **adult-onset Still's disease**.
A positive **IGRA** shows TB **exposure** only; it cannot tell latent from active disease and should prompt a search for active TB.
**GeneXpert MTB/RIF** on sputum detects _M. tuberculosis_ and rifampicin resistance.
Urine for mycobacteria needs **three early-morning samples**.

blocks.text: **PET** (FDG PET-CT) can reveal vasculitis or occult malignancy and helps **choose a biopsy site**. A tagged white-cell scan can help but does not by itself give the diagnosis.

blocks.note: Look at: common sites of infection presenting with fever, e.g. CT of a pyogenic liver abscess and a diverticular abscess, and a chest X-ray of pulmonary TB.

blocks.text: Do not scan every PUO patient from **head to toe** as a first step; use imaging selectively. **Blind biopsy** of an organ with no localising sign, lab clue or imaging abnormality is unhelpful.

First Aid calls marrow and liver biopsy **low yield**, while Davidson quotes a marrow yield of **up to 15%** and supports liver biopsy when LFTs or imaging are abnormal. Follow Davidson: biopsy when there is a pointer, not blindly.

Treat **symptoms** with **paracetamol** and **tepid sponging**, and replace **salt and water** in patients with drenching sweats. Until a firm diagnosis is made, keep treatment **symptomatic** where possible. Definitive treatment is aimed at the **underlying cause**.

blocks.title: Empirical treatment in PUO
rows: Make occult infection harder to diagnose and mask the fever pattern
Neutropenic, critically ill or very unwell patients
Can worsen an infection and mask inflammation without treating the cause
Strong suspicion of a specific rheumatological diagnosis

blocks.title: Other practical steps
items: **Stop unnecessary drugs** (possible drug fever) and **remove indwelling lines** or other potential sources.
Match the **urgency** of investigation to how ill the patient is and to their immune status.
In a stable patient, **observation alone** may reveal the diagnosis.
Patients still symptomatic without a diagnosis need repeated **re-evaluation** (history, examination, tests), **shared decision-making** and discussion at a **multidisciplinary infection meeting**.

blocks.title: When an antipyretic is clearly worthwhile (Step-Up)
items: Temperature **above 41°C**.
**Pregnancy**.
Significant **cardiopulmonary disease** (extra oxygen demand).
Symptom relief from chills or myalgia.
Hyperthermia does not respond to antipyretics. It needs **external cooling** and cause-specific drugs, e.g. **dantrolene** for malignant hyperthermia.

blocks.text: **Prognosis.** About **10%** of PUO stays undiagnosed (Davidson), but **long-term mortality is low** as long as there is no significant weight loss or sign of another disease. Most undiagnosed fevers **settle on their own**, sometimes over months to years. If no cause has emerged after **2 years**, the outlook is good.
In the undiagnosed patient, **significant weight loss** or new signs are the red flags that justify further investigation; without them, reassurance and follow-up are appropriate.

A "trial of steroids" or antibiotics to see whether the fever settles is a classic wrong answer. Steroids can let an occult infection such as **TB or an abscess** progress, and both treatments **mask the fever pattern** and the inflammatory response, delaying the diagnosis.

cards.back: Temperature **>38.0°C** on several occasions for **>3 weeks**, with no diagnosis after **1 week** of in-hospital investigation.

cards.front: The relaxed (modern) investigation requirement for PUO?
cards.back: **3 days** as an inpatient, **3 outpatient visits**, or **1 week** of intensive ambulatory investigation.

cards.front: Why does hyperthermia not respond to antipyretics?
cards.back: The hypothalamic **set-point is unchanged**; the body fails to lose heat. Treat with external cooling and cause-specific drugs (e.g. dantrolene).
Fever persisting **>2 weeks** despite intelligent, intensive investigation (Davidson: >3 weeks).

cards.front: Largest group in Davidson's PUO aetiology?
Commonest connective tissue cause of PUO in older adults?
PUO with a fleeting truncal rash, sore throat and a very high ferritin?
Name four clues to factitious fever.
cards.back: Patient looks well; no diurnal variation or pulse rise; temperature >41°C; no sweating on defervescence; normal ESR/CRP; normal supervised reading; mixed commensal organisms.

cards.front: Travel-related PUO from South-east Asia: which Davidson organism?
Diagnostic yield of bone marrow biopsy in PUO?
cards.back: **Up to 15%**: mostly haematological malignancy, myelodysplasia or TB. Send marrow for **culture** too.

cards.front: Who should be considered for temporal artery biopsy in PUO?
cards.back: Anyone **over 50**, even with no signs and a **normal ESR**.

cards.front: What can an IGRA not do?
cards.back: Distinguish **latent** from **active** TB; it only shows exposure.

cards.front: Diagnostic test of choice for visceral leishmaniasis?
Two empirical treatments to avoid in undiagnosed PUO?
cards.back: **Blind antibiotics** (unless neutropenic or critically ill) and **empirical steroids** (unless a specific rheumatological diagnosis is strongly suspected).

cards.front: Prognosis of PUO with no cause found?
cards.back: **Good**: low long-term mortality without significant weight loss; most settle, and the outlook is good if no cause appears after 2 years.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has had evening fevers of 38.4–38.7°C for 10 days. FBC, CRP, urinalysis and a chest X-ray done by his GP are unremarkable. A junior doctor writes "pyrexia of unknown origin" in the notes.
questions.leadIn: Why does he not yet meet Davidson's classic definition of PUO?
options: The fever has lasted less than 3 weeks
He has not yet had an HIV test
He has not had a PET-CT scan
The fever is not continuous through the day
questions.explanation: Davidson's classic definition needs a temperature **above 38.0°C on several occasions for more than 3 weeks**, plus investigation (1 week in hospital, or the relaxed equivalents) without a diagnosis. Ten days is too short.
whyNot: 38.3°C is the US threshold; Davidson uses 38.0°C, which he exceeds.
An HIV test belongs in the work-up, but missing it is not what excludes him from the definition.
No imaging test is part of the definition.
The definition only needs fever recorded on several occasions, not a continuous fever.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man started on an antipsychotic a week ago becomes rigid and confused, with a temperature of 40.6°C. Regular paracetamol has had no effect on his temperature.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains his raised temperature?
options: Failure to lose heat with an unchanged hypothalamic set-point
Cytokine-driven raising of the hypothalamic set-point
An exaggerated but normal circadian rhythm
Release of pyrogens from an occult abscess
questions.explanation: This is **hyperthermia** (neuroleptic malignant syndrome). The set-point is **unchanged** and heat cannot be dissipated, which is why antipyretics fail. It needs external cooling and cause-specific drugs.
whyNot: A raised set-point is true fever, which usually responds to antipyretics.
Circadian variation is mild, harmless and does not cause rigidity or 40.6°C.
Factitious fever occurs in a well-looking patient, not one who is rigid and confused.
Pyrogens from an abscess raise the set-point, so the fever would usually respond to paracetamol.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman has had 5 weeks of low-grade fever, weight loss, a new headache, aching shoulders and pain in her jaw when chewing. ESR is 96 mm/h. Blood cultures and chest X-ray are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of her PUO?
questions.explanation: Older age, headache, **jaw claudication**, shoulder-girdle aching and a very high ESR point to **GCA/PMR**, the commonest connective tissue cause of PUO in older adults in Davidson.
whyNot: Still's disease affects younger adults and gives a fleeting rash, sore throat and very high ferritin.
Endocarditis would be expected to give positive cultures or a murmur; jaw claudication is not a feature.
Lymphoma gives lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and a raised LDH, not jaw claudication.
FMF gives episodic fever with serositis, usually from a young age, often with a family history.

questions.stem: A student is summarising the aetiology of pyrexia of unknown origin from Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine.
questions.leadIn: Which group accounts for the largest share of cases?
questions.explanation: Davidson gives **infection ~30%**, malignancy ~20%, connective tissue disorders ~15%, miscellaneous ~20% and idiopathic ~15%.
whyNot: Malignancy is about 20%.
Connective tissue disorders are about 15%.
The miscellaneous group is about 20%.
Step-Up says idiopathic is now commonest, but Davidson (the course authority) puts it at about 15%.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old healthcare assistant has a temperature chart showing spikes to 41.6°C with no daily pattern. She looks well, her pulse stays around 72/min during the spikes and she does not sweat as readings fall. CRP and ESR are normal. One blood culture grew a mixture of gut organisms.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Davidson's clues to **factitious fever** are all here: a well patient, readings above 41°C, no diurnal variation, no pulse response, no sweating on defervescence, **normal inflammatory markers** and a **polymicrobial commensal** culture. Confirm with supervised readings.
whyNot: Endocarditis raises the CRP, and the patient would usually look unwell, with the pulse following the temperature.
Still's disease produces a very high ferritin and raised inflammatory markers.
Lymphoma causes genuine fever with lymphadenopathy or a raised LDH, and the ESR/CRP are usually up.
Thyrotoxicosis causes a fast pulse and sweating, often without fever.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with advanced, untreated HIV infection has had 5 weeks of fever, weight loss, anaemia and hepatosplenomegaly. Chest X-ray is normal.
questions.leadIn: Which cause should be actively sought first?
options: HIV viraemia as the sole cause
questions.explanation: In HIV-positive patients with PUO, **over 75% of causes are infectious**. AIDS-defining infections such as **disseminated MAC**, CMV and histoplasmosis head the list. Fever, weight loss, anaemia and organomegaly fit DMAC.
whyNot: HIV itself is rarely the cause of PUO; an opportunistic infection must be excluded.
FMF is an inherited periodic fever with serositis, unrelated to HIV.
PMR affects older adults with shoulder and hip girdle pain and a high ESR.
Atrial myxoma is a rare miscellaneous cause and does not explain organomegaly in advanced HIV.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has had 4 weeks of fever and weight loss. Hb is 92 g/L, WCC 2.8 × 10⁹/L and platelets 71 × 10⁹/L. Blood cultures, chest X-ray and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis show nothing.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most likely to give the diagnosis?
options: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with culture
questions.explanation: Pancytopenia points to the marrow. Bone marrow biopsy has a yield of **up to 15%** in PUO, mainly **haematological malignancy, myelodysplasia or TB**. Send it for **culture** as well as histology.
whyNot: Temporal artery biopsy is worth considering over 50, but GCA does not cause pancytopenia.
A repeat film is unlikely to add to a normal CT.
A labelled white-cell scan finds inflammation but does not explain a marrow problem.
Thyrotoxicosis is a rare cause of PUO and does not explain pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman who grew up in a TB-endemic country has PUO. An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is positive. Chest X-ray is normal.
questions.leadIn: What does the positive IGRA show?
options: Exposure to M. tuberculosis, not necessarily active disease
Cure of a previous TB infection
questions.explanation: An IGRA shows **exposure** to TB. It **cannot separate latent from active** disease, so it should only trigger a search for active TB (cultures, GeneXpert, tissue).
whyNot: A positive IGRA does not prove active disease.
Rifampicin resistance is detected by GeneXpert MTB/RIF, not by an IGRA.
An IGRA tells you nothing about cure.
IGRAs target M. tuberculosis antigens and do not diagnose MAC.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with 4 weeks of unexplained fever is haemodynamically stable and eating well. Blood cultures and a CT scan are pending. The FY1 suggests starting intravenous ceftriaxone "to cover something".
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate plan?
questions.explanation: In a stable patient, give **symptomatic treatment only** (paracetamol, sponging, fluids) until a diagnosis is made. Blind antibiotics make occult infection harder to diagnose.
whyNot: Blind antibiotics mask the fever pattern and lower culture yield; they are reserved for neutropenic or critically ill patients.
Empirical steroids can worsen infection and hide inflammation.
Treating TB without evidence also obscures the diagnosis; seek proof first (cultures, biopsy).
Nothing points to malaria, and a test (films or rapid test) should come first.

questions.stem: Each of these patients has had unexplained fever for over 3 weeks.
questions.leadIn: In which patient are empirical antibiotics justified before a diagnosis is made?
options: A 52-year-old on chemotherapy with a very low neutrophil count
A well 40-year-old with evening fevers and a normal CRP
A 70-year-old with jaw claudication and a high ESR
A 25-year-old with a fleeting rash and a very high ferritin
A 31-year-old nurse with a bizarre temperature chart
questions.explanation: Empirical antibiotics are **not indicated in PUO** except in **neutropenic** or **critically ill** patients, where delay could be fatal.
whyNot: A well patient needs observation and investigation, not blind antibiotics.
This suggests GCA, which needs temporal artery biopsy and steroids, not antibiotics.
This suggests adult-onset Still's disease, an inflammatory cause.
This suggests factitious fever; antibiotics are inappropriate.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had 6 weeks of daily high fevers with a transient rash on her trunk that appears with the fever, sore throat, joint pains and tender cervical lymph nodes. ANA is negative and serum ferritin is markedly raised.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A fleeting truncal rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy and a **very high ferritin** in a young adult is the pattern of **adult-onset Still's disease**, which Davidson marks as a commonest connective tissue cause in younger adults.
whyNot: SLE would usually give a positive ANA.
Lymphoma can cause fever and lymph nodes, but a fleeting rash with sore throat and very high ferritin fits Still's.
Endocarditis gives a murmur and positive cultures, not a fleeting rash with sore throat.
There is no history of a new drug before the fever.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has had 4 weeks of fever and weight loss. Urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria on two occasions, and his haematocrit is above the reference range. Blood cultures are negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Fever with **microscopic haematuria** and a **raised haematocrit** (erythrocytosis) is the classic pattern of **renal cell carcinoma**, a solid tumour on Davidson's malignant list.
whyNot: Lymphoma lowers rather than raises the haematocrit and gives lymphadenopathy and a high LDH.
Myxoma gives emboli and obstructive cardiac symptoms, not haematuria with erythrocytosis.
PAN can cause renal involvement but not erythrocytosis.
HCC would usually come with chronic liver disease or abnormal LFTs, not haematuria.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with 4 weeks of fever describes difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair. Creatine kinase is markedly raised. She takes no regular medicines.
questions.leadIn: Which group of causes does the raised CK point to?
questions.explanation: Follow up every abnormal result. A raised CK suggests **myositis** (polymyositis is on Davidson's connective tissue list) or a drug effect; she takes no drugs, so myositis is most likely.
whyNot: Raised liver enzymes, not CK, point to the liver or biliary tree.
Still's disease is signalled by a very high ferritin, not a high CK.
Renal cell carcinoma is suggested by haematuria and a raised haematocrit.
Thyrotoxicosis is not suggested by a markedly raised CK.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old care-home resident has become confused. Her oral temperature is 37.4°C, but a rectal reading taken soon after is 38.6°C.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about fever in old age is correct?
options: Oral readings are unreliable and can miss fever
Delirium in an older patient excludes infection
A recent stroke explains fever, so infection need not be sought
More PUO cases stay undiagnosed in older than in younger patients
Fever in older patients is usually due to viral infection
questions.explanation: In older people **oral temperatures are unreliable**, so fever can be missed; rectal or eardrum readings are better. Delirium commonly accompanies fever.
whyNot: Delirium is common during fever in older people; it suggests rather than excludes infection.
Stroke can cause fever, but co-existing infection must still be excluded.
Davidson states that fewer cases stay undiagnosed in older people than in the young.
Viral causes are more typical in children and younger adults.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman has had 6 weeks of fever and fatigue. Examination shows no localising signs, her ESR is normal, and first- and second-line tests including CT and echocardiography are unremarkable.
questions.leadIn: Which biopsy should be considered next?
questions.explanation: Davidson advises considering **temporal artery biopsy in anyone over 50**, even with **no physical signs and a normal ESR**. Blind biopsy of other organs without a pointer is unhelpful.
whyNot: Liver biopsy is justified only if LFTs or imaging are abnormal.
Laparoscopic biopsy is reserved for abnormal tissue, not a blind search.
Renal biopsy is for evidence of glomerulonephritis such as RPGN, which she does not have.
A skin biopsy needs a skin lesion to sample.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman complains of heavy sweating, palpitations, tremor and weight loss over 2 months. Her temperature is repeatedly 37.1–37.3°C.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of her sweating?
questions.explanation: Sweating with a **normal recorded temperature** is not fever. Davidson lists **thyrotoxicosis** among causes of sweating without fever (with alcohol, anxiety, diabetes, acromegaly, lymphoma and heat); tremor and palpitations fit.
whyNot: TB causes night sweats with a genuine fever.
Endocarditis causes fever, often with night sweats and a murmur.
A liver abscess causes a genuine fever and right upper quadrant signs.
Brucellosis causes an undulating genuine fever with sweats.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old engineer spent 6 months working in rural Thailand and Cambodia. He has had fever for 4 weeks, and routine blood cultures, malaria tests and dengue NS1 are negative.
questions.leadIn: Which organism on Davidson's list of geographically restricted PUO causes is linked to this region?
questions.explanation: **Melioidosis** (_Burkholderia pseudomallei_) is the PUO cause Davidson ties to **South-east Asia**.
whyNot: MERS-CoV is linked to the Arabian Peninsula.
T. cruzi is linked to Central and South America.
Coxiella is a culture-negative endocarditis organism, not a region-specific cause in this list.
T. whipplei is a fastidious organism not tied to a travel region.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has had intermittent fevers for 2½ years. Repeated full investigation, including CT, PET and marrow biopsy, has found no cause. His weight is stable and he feels well between episodes.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about his outlook is most accurate?
options: He most likely has an occult lymphoma
He should start empirical antituberculous treatment
questions.explanation: About 10% of PUO stays undiagnosed. Without **significant weight loss** or another disease, long-term mortality is low, and after **2 years** with no cause the outlook is good.
whyNot: With a stable weight and repeatedly negative tests including PET and marrow, lymphoma is unlikely.
Blind invasive procedures without a localising clue are unhelpful.
Empirical treatment without evidence is not recommended.
Empirical steroids may mask inflammation or worsen infection.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman came back 2 weeks ago from 2 months of volunteering in rural West Africa. She has had fever for over 3 weeks, starting while she was still there. She took no antimalarial prophylaxis. She has no localising symptoms.
questions.leadIn: Which initial test should be prioritised?
options: Malaria films on 3 consecutive days or a malaria rapid test
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** recognise a returning traveller with fever and no localising signs. **Step 2:** in tests for fever, Davidson adds geography-driven tests to the standard first line; for Africa, Asia and Latin America these include **malaria films on 3 consecutive days** (or an antigen RDT), **dengue NS1**, Typhi blood cultures and abdominal ultrasound. **Step 3:** malaria is a commonest infective cause and can kill, so exclude it first. Imaging and biopsy come later.
whyNot: PET-CT is a second-line test after negative initial work-up.
She is 29 and has no features of GCA.
Marrow biopsy is an invasive later step, not a first test.
Echo is a second-line test, with no murmur or other clue to suggest endocarditis yet.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old vet who handles sheep and cattle has had 6 weeks of fever, sweats and fatigue. He has splinter haemorrhages and a new early diastolic murmur. Three sets of blood cultures taken before any antibiotics show no growth after prolonged incubation. Echocardiography shows an aortic valve vegetation. ANA and antiphospholipid antibodies are negative.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** a vegetation, new regurgitant murmur and splinter haemorrhages make **endocarditis** almost certain; it is a commonest infective cause of PUO. **Step 2:** cultures taken properly are negative, so this is **culture-negative** endocarditis. **Step 3:** _Coxiella_ and _Bartonella_ are the leading culture-negative organisms, and farm-animal contact fits **Coxiella**; confirm with serology. **Step 4:** negative ANA and antiphospholipid antibodies argue against Libman–Sacks.
whyNot: Libman–Sacks lesions occur with SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome; both antibody tests are negative.
A myxoma is a mass rather than a valve vegetation and does not explain splinter haemorrhages.
Lymphoma does not cause valve vegetations.
PAN causes systemic vasculitis, not valve vegetations.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has had 4 weeks of fever. Davidson's first-line tests (FBC, U&E, LFTs, CRP, HIV test, ANA, chest X-ray, ECG, urine and blood cultures) are all normal. Repeated examination shows no localising signs.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** the first round is negative, so move to Davidson's second-line tests: mycobacterial samples, serology and ferritin, **abdominal ultrasound or CT**, and echocardiography. **Step 2:** abdominal imaging looks for an **occult abscess or tumour**, two big PUO groups. **Step 3:** biopsy should follow a lead (an imaging lesion, abnormal bloods); blind biopsy is unhelpful, and empirical steroids are avoided.
whyNot: Liver biopsy is justified only when LFTs or imaging are abnormal.
Laparotomy is invasive and is not a routine next step without a target.
Nothing points to the kidneys.
Empirical steroids may worsen an infection and mask the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man who injects heroin into his groin has fever and holds his right hip flexed. Passive extension of the hip causes severe pain and spasm. There is no joint effusion.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Femoral injection risks local complications including **ilio-psoas abscess**. A flexed hip with pain on passive extension (a positive **femoral stretch test**) is the classic sign (Davidson Fig. 11.2).
whyNot: A septic DVT causes leg swelling, not hip flexor spasm.
Tricuspid endocarditis causes fever and septic lung emboli, not hip flexion.
A disc prolapse is not associated with fever in an injection drug user.
Necrotising fasciitis gives extreme pain, bullae and skin change.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with PUO received several courses of oral antibiotics from her GP. CT now shows a vertebral lesion, and a biopsy is sent for culture, but nothing grows.
questions.leadIn: Which test on the biopsy may still identify the organism?
questions.explanation: After antibiotics, cultures often fail. **16S rRNA analysis** of the tissue detects bacterial DNA and can name the organism.
whyNot: An IGRA is a blood test showing TB exposure; it does not identify an organism in tissue.
ESR is a non-specific inflammatory marker.
Ferritin is a clue to Still's disease, not a microbiological test.
ANA screens for connective tissue disease.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has had attacks lasting 2–3 days of fever with severe abdominal pain and pleuritic chest pain since his teens. WBC and ESR rise during attacks and are normal in between. His uncle had similar episodes.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Familial Mediterranean fever** gives episodic fever with **peritonitis and pleuritis**, inflammatory markers that rise in attacks, and a **family history** (a periodic fever syndrome).
whyNot: Factitious fever comes with normal inflammatory markers.
Lymphoma does not cause brief, self-limiting serositis attacks since the teens.
Still's disease gives a fleeting rash, sore throat and high ferritin, not recurrent serositis.
TB peritonitis is persistent, not a series of brief attacks over years.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man from Bihar, India, has had 2 months of fever, weight loss and massive splenomegaly, with pancytopenia. He is under a specialist tropical medicine unit.
questions.leadIn: What is the diagnostic test of choice for the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: This suggests **visceral leishmaniasis**. In specialist centres, **splenic aspiration** is the test of choice.
whyNot: Marrow can show Leishmania, but splenic aspiration is the test of choice in specialist centres.
GCA does not cause massive splenomegaly in a 33-year-old.
There is no lymphadenopathy to sample.
Liver biopsy is not the preferred test for leishmaniasis.

questions.stem: A UK textbook and Davidson differ in how long a fever must last before it is called PUO.
questions.leadIn: What minimum duration does Kumar & Clark use?
questions.explanation: Kumar & Clark use a fever lasting **more than 2 weeks** despite intelligent, intensive investigation. Davidson (the course authority) uses **more than 3 weeks**.
whyNot: One week is the classic length of inpatient investigation, not the fever duration.
More than 3 weeks is Davidson's duration, not Kumar & Clark's.
No source uses 6 weeks.
No source uses 3 months.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man under investigation for PUO has drenching night sweats every night. He now feels faint on standing, has a postural blood pressure drop and his urea has risen.
questions.leadIn: Along with paracetamol, what supportive measure is most needed?
questions.explanation: Davidson's symptomatic care is **paracetamol, tepid sponging and salt and water replacement** for drenching sweats. This man is volume depleted.
whyNot: Blind antibiotics hinder diagnosis and do not correct dehydration.
Steroids may mask inflammation and worsen infection.
He is volume depleted; restricting fluid would worsen this.
A diuretic would worsen dehydration.

questions.theme: Causes of pyrexia of unknown origin
questions.leadIn: For each patient with prolonged unexplained fever, pick the most likely cause. An option can be the answer to one item, to several items, or to none.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man was started on procainamide for an arrhythmia 10 days before his fevers began. He looks well, examination is normal, and blood cultures, chest X-ray and abdominal CT are unremarkable.
items.explanation: Fever that begins soon after a **new drug** (procainamide is a recognised culprit), with a normal work-up, suggests **drug fever**. Stop the drug; the fever should settle.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has fever, weight loss and intermittent breathlessness. She recently had a transient episode of left arm weakness. Blood cultures are repeatedly negative.
items.explanation: Constitutional upset, **obstructive** symptoms and **embolic** events are the pattern of **atrial myxoma**. Echocardiography will show it.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has 6 weeks of fever and night sweats. He has enlarged cervical and axillary lymph nodes and a palpable spleen. Platelets are low and LDH is raised.
items.explanation: Lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, **low platelets** and a **high LDH** point to **lymphoma**. Excision node biopsy is needed, sometimes more than once.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man who moved from Pakistan 2 years ago has had fever and weight loss for 7 weeks. Chest X-ray and sputum smears are normal. Raised ALP prompts a liver biopsy, which shows granulomas; mycobacteria later grow in culture.
items.explanation: Two steps: granulomas on liver biopsy (granulomatous hepatitis) narrow the field, and a **positive mycobacterial culture** confirms **extrapulmonary TB**. A normal CXR and smears do not exclude disseminated TB.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man has had 4 weeks of fever with vague perineal ache and occasional dysuria. Two standard urine cultures, blood cultures and an abdominal CT are unremarkable.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most likely to reveal the source?
questions.explanation: Davidson reminds us that in men the **prostate** can be a hidden source, and lists **urine culture after prostatic massage** in older men. The perineal ache and dysuria point there.
whyNot: Temporal artery biopsy is reasonable over 50 without a source, but his symptoms point to the prostate.
Marrow biopsy is for cytopenias or suspected haematological disease.
PET-CT is useful when no clue exists; here a simple targeted test comes first.
Echo targets endocarditis, with no murmur or embolic clue here.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has PUO with a persistently high ESR and CRP. Examination, CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, echocardiography and a temporal artery biopsy are all unremarkable.
questions.leadIn: Which imaging test could reveal a large-vessel vasculitis or guide a biopsy?
questions.explanation: **PET** can help diagnose **vasculitis** (including aortitis) and pick a **biopsy site**; FDG PET-CT also finds occult malignancy and inflammation.
whyNot: A plain abdominal film adds nothing after a normal CT.
A normal CT chest makes a repeat chest X-ray pointless.
A bone scan looks at the skeleton, not vessel walls.
Thyroid ultrasound would not show vasculitis.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old shepherd from a Mediterranean village has 2 months of fever, hepatosplenomegaly and mild pancytopenia. Blood cultures so far are negative. The haematologist will perform a bone marrow aspirate and trephine.
questions.leadIn: How should the marrow sample be handled to give the best diagnostic yield?
options: Sent for culture as well as microscopy and histology
Stored until blood cultures are final
questions.explanation: Marrow can reveal **brucellosis, typhoid, visceral leishmaniasis and TB** as well as haematological malignancy. Davidson stresses sending marrow for **culture** as well as microscopy. This shepherd's exposure makes **Brucella** likely.
whyNot: Histology alone misses organisms that only grow in culture, such as Brucella.
Cytogenetics looks only for haematological malignancy.
Waiting wastes the sample; send it fresh for culture.
Flow cytometry only addresses haematological malignancy.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has had 5 weeks of fever with a high ESR. Extensive tests have not found a cause. A colleague suggests a "trial of prednisolone to see whether the fever settles".
questions.leadIn: What is the best response?
options: Avoid steroids until a specific diagnosis is made
questions.explanation: **Empirical steroids** may **worsen an occult infection** (e.g. TB) or **mask inflammation** and the fever pattern without treating the cause. Use them only when a specific rheumatological diagnosis is strongly suspected.
whyNot: High-dose steroids can let an infection progress and hide the diagnosis.
Even a low dose can mask the fever pattern and inflammatory markers.
Adding blind antibiotics compounds the problem: both mask the diagnosis.
Undiagnosed patients need continued re-evaluation, not closure of the work-up.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has had a recorded fever above 38°C on several occasions for 4 weeks. She has not been admitted to hospital.
questions.leadIn: Under Davidson's relaxed definition, which amount of investigation without a diagnosis would make this PUO?
options: One set of normal blood tests
questions.explanation: The relaxed definition accepts **3 days of inpatient care, 3 outpatient visits, or 1 week of intensive ambulatory investigation** in place of the classic week in hospital.
whyNot: One visit is not enough investigation.
The inpatient option needs 3 days.
A single scan does not meet the requirement.
One set of blood tests does not meet the requirement.

ospe.identify: Abdominal CT showing a **pyogenic liver abscess**: one of the common abdominal infections that present with fever.
Abdominal CT showing a **diverticular abscess**: an intra-abdominal infection that can present with fever.
Chest X-ray of **pulmonary tuberculosis**, one of the common respiratory infections that present with fever.
Injection drug user with **hip flexor spasm** from an **ilio-psoas abscess**, and **skin abscesses** at injection sites. Also look for splinter haemorrhages and Roth's spots (endocarditis).
